scenarios.title: Scenario 3 — Multi-Agent Research System
scenarios.domains: D1 Agentic Architecture · D2 Tool Design & MCP · D5 Context & Reliability
scenarios.brief: A hospital network's evidence team runs a research system on the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator delegates through the Task tool to subagents for literature search, trial-registry search, document analysis, citation checking, synthesis and reporting. Journals and the trial registry are reached over MCP. Evidence summaries go to clinical guideline committees, and every claim must cite a paper and section.

scenarios.title: Scenario 4 — Developer Productivity with Claude
scenarios.domains: D1 Agentic Architecture · D2 Tool Design & MCP · D3 Claude Code Configuration
scenarios.brief: A language-learning app company's platform team uses Claude Code on a Ruby on Rails monolith with a React front end. Engineers explore and change code with the built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob), plus MCP servers for Linear and a staging Postgres database. Some engineers also script Claude through the Agent SDK for internal tools.

questions.question: The team wrote its own coordinator loop. After each response, the loop checks whether the response contains a text block. If it does, the loop treats the run as finished and sends that text to the report subagent. Runs often stop after the first search. In those runs, Claude wrote a short sentence and requested more Task calls in the same response. Which change fixes the loop?

options.t: Base the loop's exit on each response's stop_reason, continuing on tool_use and exiting only on end_turn.
options.why: Correct. stop_reason is the loop's signal. A response can hold a sentence and tool calls together; stop_reason tool_use says the model still wants those calls run.

options.t: Set tool_choice to any on the coordinator's requests until the report subagent has run, then return to auto.
options.why: Runner-up. any is the fix when Claude answers in text instead of calling a tool. Here Claude did call tools; the loop ignored them, and any would also stop Claude ending the run normally.

options.t: Exit only when the response's last content block is text, after running any tool_use blocks that precede it.
options.why: Incorrect. Still a text-content check. Claude can end a response with text while asking for more work, and block order is not the API's completion signal.

options.t: Cap the loop at a turn budget set for each request type, and pass the last text block to the report subagent.
options.why: Incorrect. An iteration cap as the main stop rule is an anti-pattern; it cuts off long runs and wastes turns on short ones.

questions.decider: Claude's stopping response also contained Task calls, so stop_reason was tool_use; if Claude had replied with text only and no tool calls, forcing a tool call with tool_choice any would be the fix.
questions.explanation: The agentic loop continues while stop_reason is tool_use and ends on end_turn. Checking for text in the reply is an unreliable completion signal, because Claude often writes a sentence before its tool calls.

eli5.question: The loop stops too early. The question asks how to fix the loop's stop rule. The clue is: Claude wrote a short sentence and requested more Task calls in the same response.
eli5.answer: Think of a waiter who leaves the table as soon as you say anything, even "hmm, and also…". You were still ordering. The API tells you plainly whether Claude is still ordering: a field called stop_reason. If it says tool_use, run the tools and go round again. If it says end_turn, Claude is done. Rule: loop on stop_reason, not on what the text looks like.
options: Correct. Use the official signal: keep going on tool_use, stop on end_turn.
Runner-up. Forcing a tool call (tool_choice: any) helps when Claude talks instead of acting. Here Claude did act; the loop just didn't listen.
Checking whether the last block is text is still reading the text, not the official signal.
A turn budget stops at an arbitrary point, finished or not.

deep.premise: It is tempting to read "a text reply" as "the final answer". In the API it isn't. One response can hold a text block and tool_use blocks. The only reliable signal for "done" is stop_reason: tool_use means run the tools and continue, end_turn means finished.
deep.diagram:
response = [text: "Next I'll search...", tool_use, tool_use]
stop_reason = "tool_use"  -> run tools, loop again
stop_reason = "end_turn"  -> finished

questions.obj: 1.3 Per-request context in the Task prompt
questions.question: Each committee sets its own inclusion rules when it submits a request, such as a minimum trial size or excluded drug classes. The coordinator agrees these rules with the requester before delegating. The analysis subagent then includes studies the committee excluded. Its Task prompt names the drug and the outcome, but nothing else. The rules differ on every request. Where should the inclusion rules go?

options.t: Into the analysis subagent's AgentDefinition system prompt, as a criteria section with included and excluded examples.
options.why: Runner-up. A subagent's system prompt is the right home for criteria that are the same on every run. These change per request, so a fixed prompt can't hold them.

options.t: Into a criteria section of the coordinator's system prompt, which the coordinator updates for each new request.
options.why: Incorrect. The coordinator's prompt is part of the coordinator's context. Subagents don't inherit it, so the analysis step still never sees the rules.

options.t: Into a case-facts block the coordinator maintains, listing the drug, the outcome and each inclusion rule.
options.why: Incorrect. A case-facts block keeps details safe in the coordinator's own long context. It doesn't reach a subagent unless it is written into the delegation.

options.t: Into each analysis Task prompt, stated in full for that request beside the drug and the outcome to study.
options.why: Correct. Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's conversation; per-request context must be passed explicitly in the Task prompt.

questions.decider: The rules differ on every request, so they must travel in each Task prompt; if every committee used the same fixed rules, the subagent's system prompt would be the better home.
questions.explanation: Subagents have isolated context and do not see what the coordinator discussed. Anything specific to one request must be written into that delegation's prompt; fixed role guidance belongs in the AgentDefinition.

eli5.question: A helper ignores rules that the boss agreed with the customer. The question asks where those rules should be written. The clue is: the rules differ on every request.
eli5.answer: Picture a kitchen. The head chef took the customer's allergy note, but the cook only got a ticket saying "pasta". The cook can't see the chef's conversation (subagents have isolated context). So the allergy note must go on the ticket itself: the Task prompt. A note pinned on the cook's wall (the system prompt) only works for rules that never change. Rule: per-request facts go in the Task prompt; fixed role rules go in the system prompt.
options: Runner-up. The wall note (system prompt) is right for rules that are the same every time. These change per request.
The boss's own notes (coordinator's system prompt) stay with the boss. The cook never sees them.
A fact sheet (case-facts block) on the boss's desk is still on the boss's desk.
Correct. Write this request's rules on this request's ticket.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the subagent "knows" what the coordinator agreed, so the fix must be better instructions in general. It doesn't know. Subagents start with only their own system prompt and the Task prompt. The real choice is which of those two the rules belong in, and that depends on whether the rules change.

guide.obj: 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
guide.quote: Subagent context must be provided explicitly in the prompt (no automatic inheritance / shared memory).

questions.question: For each request, the coordinator runs three searches: journal literature, the trial registry and regulatory notices. None of the searches uses another's results. Today the coordinator sends one Task call, waits for its result, then sends the next. Committees say summaries take too long. Every request needs all three searches. Which change best cuts the wait?

options.t: Let the coordinator judge each request's complexity and invoke only the search subagents that request needs.
options.why: Runner-up. Dynamic selection saves time when many requests skip some subagents. Here every request needs all three.

options.t: Have the coordinator emit the three Task calls together in one response and use each result as it arrives.
options.why: Correct. Independent subagents can run in parallel when the coordinator emits multiple Task calls in a single response.

options.t: Merge the three search subagents into one that holds all three search tools and runs the searches itself.
options.why: Incorrect. One subagent with all the tools still runs the searches one after another, and it mixes three roles in one context.

options.t: Have each search subagent return only trimmed fields, so the coordinator reads less from each result.
options.why: Incorrect. Trimming saves context tokens, but the wait comes from running independent searches in series.

questions.decider: Every request needs all three independent searches, so the time goes to running them one after another; if many requests needed only some searches, selecting subagents per request would cut more.
questions.explanation: Independent subtasks should run in parallel: the coordinator emits several Task calls in one response. Dynamic selection helps only when some subagents are unnecessary for a request.

eli5.question: Three independent searches run one after another, and summaries are slow. The question asks for the best way to cut the wait. The clue is: every request needs all three searches.
eli5.answer: Think of three shopping errands that don't depend on each other. Sending one friend, waiting, then sending the next is slow. Send all three friends at once. In the Agent SDK, the coordinator does this by putting several Task calls in one response. Skipping errands would help only if some were unnecessary, and here none are. Rule: independent subtasks go out together, in one response.
options: Runner-up. Skipping helpers (dynamic selection) helps when some aren't needed. All three are needed here.
Correct. Send all three at once; they don't depend on each other.
One helper doing all three errands (merged subagent) still does them one after another.
Shorter reports back (trimming) save reading, but the helpers still go out one at a time.

deep.premise: It is tempting to treat "too slow" as "doing too much" and reach for skipping work. But nothing here is unnecessary. The time is lost because independent work runs in series. The fix is parallelism, not less work.

questions.question: The coordinator publishes each summary by calling publish_summary. Policy says no summary may reach a committee until the citation-check subagent has passed every citation in it. In a small share of runs, the coordinator publishes before the check has run. Each such run is a reportable compliance incident. Which change meets the policy?

options.t: Force tool_choice to the citation-check delegation on the coordinator request that comes before each publish.
options.why: Incorrect. Forcing a tool works per request, but the coordinator decides when it is about to publish. A run that publishes early never reaches that forced request.

options.t: Add a PostToolUse hook on publish_summary that runs the citation check on each summary once published.
options.why: Incorrect. A hook is deterministic, but PostToolUse runs after the call. The summary has already reached the committee.

options.t: Make publish_summary refuse any draft that has no passing result on record from the citation-check subagent.
options.why: Correct. A programmatic prerequisite blocks the downstream call until the earlier step has completed, every time.

options.t: State in the coordinator prompt, as a hard requirement with its reason, that publishing waits for a passing check.
options.why: Runner-up. A clear requirement with its reason is the right prompt-level fix when occasional misses are tolerable. Prompt instructions still have a non-zero failure rate, and every miss is an incident.

questions.decider: Each early publish is a compliance incident, so the order must hold on every run; if the check were a quality goal that tolerated occasional misses, stating it as a coordinator quality criterion would be enough.
questions.explanation: When a step must happen before another every time, enforce it in code: block the downstream tool until the prerequisite has a recorded result. Prompt instructions and examples have a non-zero failure rate.

eli5.question: Sometimes a report goes out before its citations were checked. The question asks which change meets the policy. The clue is: each such run is a reportable compliance incident.
eli5.answer: Think of a lab that must not release a sample until it has passed testing. A poster saying "test first" helps, but people still forget. A lock on the release door that opens only with a pass slip never forgets. In software, that lock is a prerequisite gate: the publish code refuses unless a passing check is on record. Rule: if it must happen every time, use code, not a request.
options: Forcing a tool on one request (forced tool_choice) only helps if the run reaches that request. Early publishers skip it.
A check after release (PostToolUse hook) is automatic, but too late: the summary already went out.
Correct. The lock on the door: no pass on record, no publish.
Runner-up. A firm, well-explained instruction helps a lot. For a rule that can never be broken, you need the lock.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a better-written prompt fixes an ordering mistake. Better prompts do lower the error rate. But this policy treats every miss as an incident, and any prompt has a non-zero failure rate. When the requirement is "every time", the fix moves from words to code.

guide.obj: 1.4 Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
guide.quote: When deterministic compliance is required (e.g., identity verification before financial ops), prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate.

questions.question: Every evidence summary follows the committee template. It has the same four sections, each researched the same way: efficacy, safety, cost and guideline status. No section's research depends on what another section finds. Auditors must be able to replay each run step by step and see the same structure. The team is redesigning how the coordinator splits up work. Which decomposition fits best?

options.t: Chain fixed steps for each section in a set order, then run one integration pass over the four outputs.
options.why: Correct. When the steps are known in advance and don't depend on intermediate findings, a fixed pipeline (prompt chaining) is predictable and auditable.

options.t: Let the coordinator plan from early findings and add subtasks for each section as results come back.
options.why: Runner-up. Adaptive decomposition fits open-ended investigations where findings decide the next step. Here the steps never change, and audit needs repeatable runs.

options.t: Draft all four sections, have the coordinator check the draft for gaps, and re-delegate any thin section.
options.why: Incorrect. A refinement loop helps when coverage gaps appear. It makes run length vary, which works against step-by-step replay.

options.t: Let the coordinator size each request and invoke only the subagents that its four sections need.
options.why: Incorrect. Dynamic selection suits requests of varying size. Every request here has the same four sections.

questions.decider: The sections are fixed, independent and must replay identically for audit; if the work were open-ended and the next step depended on what was found, adaptive decomposition would win.
questions.explanation: Fixed sequential pipelines suit work whose steps are known in advance; adaptive decomposition suits investigations whose subtasks depend on intermediate findings. Predictability and auditability favour the fixed pipeline.

eli5.question: The team is choosing how to split up the research. The question asks which style fits this work. The clue is: no section's research depends on what another section finds, and auditors must replay each run.
eli5.answer: Think of a recipe card versus a detective. A recipe card (a fixed pipeline) does the same steps every time, so anyone can check it. A detective (adaptive decomposition) picks the next step from each clue. These summaries always have the same four parts done the same way, and auditors want the same steps every time. That is a recipe card. Rule: known steps use a fixed pipeline; steps that depend on findings use an adaptive plan.
options: Correct. Same steps every run, easy to replay, then one pass to join the parts.
Runner-up. The detective style wins when each finding decides the next step. Here nothing does.
A check-and-redo loop (refinement loop) fixes gaps, but makes runs vary in length.
Choosing helpers per request (dynamic selection) fits requests of different sizes. These are all the same shape.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the adaptive approach is always the more advanced, better choice. It isn't better here. Adaptive plans shine when you can't know the steps in advance. When the steps are fixed and auditors need identical runs, a fixed pipeline is the right tool, and adaptivity becomes a cost.

questions.trap: More context or reasoning instead of structure
questions.question: The team's coordinator loop sends each request with the system prompt, the original question and only the latest tool result. Earlier turns are dropped. The coordinator often repeats searches it already ran in the same run. Runs are short and use a small part of the context window. What should the team change first?

options.t: Write each search and its findings to a scratchpad file, and have the coordinator read it before each turn.
options.why: Runner-up. A scratchpad preserves findings across context limits or session boundaries. These runs are short, so the normal message history fits and the root fault is that it's discarded.

options.t: Keep a case-facts block listing each search already run, and send it with the latest tool result.
options.why: Incorrect. A case-facts block protects key details in long conversations. Here it patches the missing history instead of restoring it, and the reasoning between turns is still lost.

options.t: Have each search tool return its cached result when it receives a query it already answered in the run.
options.why: Incorrect. Caching makes repeats cheaper but leaves Claude blind to what it already did; it treats the symptom.

options.t: Send the full message list each turn, with every assistant turn and tool result appended in order.
options.why: Correct. Tool results are appended to the conversation history so the model can reason about its next action from what it has already done.

questions.decider: The runs are short and fit easily in context, so the plain message history is the fix; if runs were long enough to exhaust the context window, an external scratchpad would be needed.
questions.explanation: In the agentic loop, each tool result is appended to the conversation history and sent back on the next request. Without it, the model cannot know what it has already done and repeats work.

eli5.question: The coordinator repeats searches it already did. The question asks what to fix first. The clue is: runs are short and use a small part of the context window.
eli5.answer: Imagine a cook who is handed only the last note from the kitchen, never the earlier ones. They'll keep asking for things they already got. The fix is to hand them the whole stack of notes: the message history with every tool result appended. Extra notebooks (a scratchpad file) are for very long jobs that outgrow the stack. These runs are short. Rule: append every tool result to the conversation; reach for external memory only when context runs out.
options: Runner-up. A scratchpad file helps when the history is too long to keep. Here it fits easily.
A list of searches done (case-facts block) is a patch. The full history is what's missing.
A cache makes repeats cheap but doesn't stop them.
Correct. Send the whole conversation, including every tool result, each time.

deep.premise: It is tempting to see repeated work and think "memory problem, add a memory tool". But the model has no memory beyond the messages you send. Here the loop throws the history away. Restore the history first; external memory is for when history no longer fits.

questions.obj: 2.3 Forcing a tool to run first
questions.question: The document-analysis subagent has two tools: extract_citation_metadata and analyze_findings. Each paper must go through extraction first, because analysis needs its page and DOI fields. The subagent calls a tool on every turn. But on some papers it calls analyze_findings first, and those findings carry no page numbers. Which setting fixes this most directly?

options.t: Rewrite both tool descriptions to say which tool comes first and which fields the analysis step expects.
options.why: Incorrect. Better descriptions improve selection but stay probabilistic; the order is still left to the model.

options.t: On the first request for each paper, set tool_choice to the named tool for metadata extraction.
options.why: Correct. A forced tool_choice makes Claude call that specific tool, so extraction runs before analysis.

options.t: Add a PostToolUse hook that looks up page and DOI fields and adds them to each analysis result.
options.why: Incorrect. A hook can transform results, but repairing them afterwards hides the skipped step instead of preventing it.

options.t: Set tool_choice to any for every request the subagent makes while it is working on a paper.
options.why: Runner-up. any guarantees a tool call instead of text. The subagent already calls a tool every turn; it picks the wrong one first.

questions.decider: The subagent already calls a tool every turn but picks the wrong one first; if it were answering in plain text instead of calling tools, tool_choice any would be the fix.
questions.explanation: tool_choice auto lets Claude choose, any forces some tool call, and a forced named tool makes Claude call that exact tool. To make a specific tool run first, force it on that request.

eli5.question: A helper sometimes skips the first step and goes straight to the second tool. The question asks which setting fixes the order. The clue is: the subagent calls a tool on every turn.
eli5.answer: Think of a form with "fill in section A first". Saying "you must use a pen" (any) doesn't help: they already use a pen. You need "start with section A" (a forced tool choice naming the tool). In the API, tool_choice can name one tool, and Claude must call exactly that one. Do that on the paper's first request, then let it choose freely. Rule: any = some tool; named = this tool.
options: Clearer labels (descriptions) help, but the model may still choose the wrong order.
Correct. Name the extraction tool for the first request, so it always starts there.
A clean-up step afterwards (PostToolUse hook) patches results instead of fixing the order.
Runner-up. any stops plain-text replies. This helper already calls tools; it just picks the wrong one first.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think tool_choice: "any" means "make it use the tools properly". It only means "call some tool, not text". When the problem is which tool comes first, you need the forced form that names the tool.

questions.obj: 1.5 Hooks that block outgoing tool calls
questions.question: An Agent SDK script lets Claude investigate data bugs on the staging database through the MCP tool run_sql. Claude needs run_sql for many read queries in each investigation. Statements that change data must never run from this script. Last week Claude ran a DELETE that wiped a tester's data. Which control should the team add?

options.t: A system prompt rule naming the allowed statement types, with examples of write requests it must refuse.
options.why: Incorrect. Prompt instructions are probabilistic; a rule that must hold every time needs code.

options.t: A permission rule in the script's settings that asks the engineer to approve each run_sql call.
options.why: Incorrect. Human approval can stop writes, but it interrupts every one of the many read queries; it is disproportionate to the need.

options.t: A hook on outgoing run_sql calls that blocks any statement other than a read and tells Claude why.
options.why: Correct. A hook that intercepts outgoing tool calls enforces the policy deterministically and lets Claude adjust.

options.t: A PostToolUse hook on run_sql that inspects the affected-row count and stops the script after any change.
options.why: Runner-up. PostToolUse hooks are the right tool for inspecting or transforming results. They run after the call, so the first write has already happened.

questions.decider: Write statements must never run, so the check has to happen before the call executes; if the goal were to inspect or normalize results, a PostToolUse hook would be right.
questions.explanation: Hooks give deterministic guarantees. Intercept outgoing tool calls to block policy-violating actions; PostToolUse hooks act on results after the call has run.

eli5.question: Claude must be able to read data but never change it. The question asks which control to add. The clue is: statements that change data must never run.
eli5.answer: Think of a bank teller. A sign saying "no withdrawals over the limit" (a prompt rule) helps but can be ignored. A teller who checks the slip before handing over cash (a hook on outgoing calls) stops it every time. Counting the money after it's gone (PostToolUse) only tells you it happened. Rule: to stop an action, check it before it runs.
options: A sign (prompt rule) makes it less likely, not impossible.
Asking a person to approve every call (approval prompt) stops writes but stalls all the reads too.
Correct. Check every statement before it runs, and block anything that writes.
Runner-up. Checking results afterwards (PostToolUse) can stop the next mistake, not the first one.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think "use a hook" settles it. Which hook matters. A PostToolUse hook runs after the tool has executed: perfect for cleaning results, useless for stopping a DELETE. To prevent an action, intercept the outgoing call.

questions.obj: 1.1 Model-driven tool use vs fixed sequence
questions.question: An internal Agent SDK tool answers engineers' questions about the codebase. Its code runs a fixed sequence: Grep for the question's keywords, Read the top three hits, then ask Claude to answer. Answers fail when the logic sits in files those hits call into. Which files matter next depends on what each Read reveals. Which TWO changes should the redesign include?

options.t: Give Claude the Grep and Read tools, and let it pick each next call from what earlier results showed.
options.why: Correct. Model-driven tool use lets Claude choose the next file from what it just read, which suits a trail that unfolds.

options.t: Keep the sequence, but add a step that follows the top hits' imports two levels deep before Claude answers.
options.why: Runner-up. A fixed chain is right when the steps are known in advance. Here the next file depends on each read, so any fixed depth is a guess.

options.t: Run the fixed sequence once per keyword in parallel subagents, and merge their reads before Claude answers.
options.why: Incorrect. Parallel subagents widen the search, but each still runs the same fixed steps and stops short of the trail.

options.t: Append each tool result to the conversation, and keep looping while stop_reason is tool_use.
options.why: Correct. The loop feeds each result back and runs until Claude signals end_turn, so Claude decides when it has enough.

questions.decider: Which files matter depends on what each Read reveals, so Claude must choose its own calls inside a stop_reason loop; if the needed files were always the same known steps, a longer fixed chain would do.
questions.explanation: Agentic loops let the model decide the next tool call from results appended to its history, continuing on tool_use and stopping on end_turn. Pre-configured sequences suit work whose steps are known in advance.

eli5.question: A tool that always does the same three steps misses answers hidden deeper in the code. The question asks which two changes make a better design. The clue is: which files matter next depends on what each Read reveals.
eli5.answer: Think of following a trail of clues. A fixed plan ("check three places, then answer") stops before the trail ends. A detective reads each clue, decides where to look next, and stops when the case is solved. In the Agent SDK that takes two parts: Claude chooses each tool call, and a loop feeds every result back until stop_reason says it is done. Rule: if the next step depends on what you just found, let the model choose, in a stop_reason loop.
options: Correct. Claude picks where to look next.
Runner-up. A deeper fixed plan works when you know how deep to go. Here the trail decides.
More helpers running the same fixed plan still can't follow clues.
Correct. Feed each result back and keep going until Claude says it's done.

deep.premise: It is tempting to fix a fixed sequence by adding one more fixed step. That works when you know what the next step is. When the next file depends on what the last read revealed, any fixed sequence eventually stops short. The model must drive, and the loop must keep feeding it results until it says it is finished.
